div.head: Attachment 1

p.hi: Objectives of International Cooperation in Space Activities

div.p: The broad objectives of the United States in international cooperation in space activities may be stated in terms of four areas of national interest (1) advancement in science and technology, (2) foreign policy, (3) national security and (4) avoiding long term economic disadvantage, including domestic considerations. They are interdependent and, therefore, no relative priority can be established among them. Rather, the suitability of each cooperative space activity must be judged within the framework of all the objectives.

These broad objectives will be sought through arrangements consistent with the President’s directive of June 1, 1972, that future joint programs should stress joint payload and utilization activities and that joint development and production in the non-payload area not be undertaken.

Since successful cooperative space activity clearly requires the engagement of significant interests on both sides—whether scientific, technical, commercial or political—it must be recognized that all these objectives may not be fully achieved in any given cooperative effort. We must expect to give as well as gain advantages to achieve real cooperation of mutual interest.

list.label: a.
list.item: To foster cooperation in basic scientific research.
list.label: b.
list.item: To develop precedents and experience in substantial cooperative undertakings which will lend themselves to other international scientific and technological activities.
list.label: c.
list.item: To obtain support and assistance in the development of our national program through (1) acquisition of scientific and technical input from areas of excellence abroad and (2) use of facilities abroad that are necessary for mission support—tracking stations, overflights, contingency recovery, etc..

list.label: a.
list.item: To encourage other countries to associate their interests with our space program.
list.label: b.
list.item: To enhance U.S. prestige and our image abroad as the world’s leader in science and technology.
list.label: c.
list.item: To seek maximum U.S. influence over the development and use of space capabilities by other countries through foreign participation in U.S. space activities and U.S. participation in space activities abroad.
list.label: d.
list.item:
To assist in the achievement of broader foreign policy objectives through: (1)
Strengthening our allies and improving our working relationships with them. (2)
Promoting multilateral cooperation with, and among, other nations. In particular, to encourage continued development of European multilateral space organizations through suitable cooperation with their programs, or a commercial or joint-program basis, in the event they desire such cooperation. (3)
Contributing to East-West detente. (4)
Enlarging economic and social benefits. (5)
Enhancing the sense of world community.

list.label: a.
list.item: To maintain the U.S. margin of advantage in technology of significance to our national security, and to avoid release of space hardware and technology which is considered to involve a disproportionate risk to our national security.
list.label: b.
list.item: To avoid proliferation of foreign capabilities to develop and deploy advanced weapons systems.

list.label: a.
b.
list.item: To promote economic benefits for the U.S. through increased exports and trade, through foreign purchases of goods and services, and through increased utilization of space and space technology.
list.label: c.
list.item: To seek opportunities to enhance our overall competitive position in space technology.
list.label: d.
list.item: To seek more productive aggregate use of American and foreign resources and skills.
list.label: e.
list.item: To seek foreign financial participation in our space payload.
list.label: f.
list.item: To enhance the cost-effectiveness of space systems through increased and more effective use.
